subsubtopic: NEED FOR FOOD BANKS CONDEMNED
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, last night Liberal Leader John Turner and Hamilton Mountain Liberal Beth Phinney had a first-hand chance to see how poverty is affecting the people on Hamilton Mountain. They visited the Neighbour-To-Neighbour Food Centre on Hamilton Mountain. I think it is a crying shame that in this day of plenty in 1987, ridings across this country should have to open food banks in order to feed our poor and hungry.
The Government in the last three Budgets has taken more money out of the hands of the poor, the working class and ordinary Canadians, and put it into the hands of rich Canadians. Now the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) has the nerve to talk about tax reform. We saw the reality last night on Hamilton Mountain. When our candidate Beth Phinney took our Leader to the food banks, she was able to show him that it is not only in the cities people are hurting. People are hurting in the suburbs. They are hurting in every riding across the country.
I think it is imperative that the Government come out with a national attack on poverty to ensure that in 1987 people do not have to stand in line for food for themselves, for their children and for their families. That is a decent policy, that is a Liberal policy, and that is the policy that Beth Phinney is going to promote when she comes here to Ottawa.

subtopic: CHALLENGE 87 JOB OPPORTUNITIES FOR YOUTH IN NORTHERN ONTARIO
CHALLENGE 87 JOB OPPORTUNITIES FOR YOUTH IN NORTHERN ONTARIO
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, much has been said in the House recently about Challenge '87 and youth job creation. I rise today to commend the Minister of State for Youth (Mr. Charest) for his fine job in furthering
the federal Government's attempt to provide meaningful job opportunities for the youth of our country.
Last year I was pleased to see how successful Challenge '86 was for northern Ontario youth. Over $8.2 million was contracted to northern Ontario under the program which resulted in creation of 4,600 jobs. Students from across the North greatly benefited from Challenge '86, and this year students will have the same enjoyment of this successful program.
I am very happy to see that the federal Government has recognized the special needs of youth in northern Ontario, and we have responded. Again I commend the Minister of State for Youth for his efforts in recognizing the regions of our country, and the Government of Canada for the employment of our youth.

Mr. Speaker, yesterday Canadians finally received a clear picture of who is really pushing for free trade in Canada. It is a Liberal-Conservative big business alliance which drew itself together with Donald Macdonald, Peter Lougheed, people such as Philippe de Gaspe Beaubien, and people supporting them from all of the major corporate groups in the country.
I wish to place on the record the voice of someone from central Saskatchewan, someone from the riding of the Minister of Justice (Mr. Hnatyshyn) who wrote to the Minister saying:
I believe it is a mistake to attempt to negotiate a free trade deal with the U.S.
while there are such strong protectionist sentiments down there . . . We don't
want to sell the farm to buy a shovel.
He goes on to make a very strong case and concludes:
Mr. Reisman should be instructed to quietly pack up and come back home.
That is the position of our Party, too.
5. O. 21 FINANCE

March 20, 1987

subtopic: PHASING OUT OF INVESTMENT TAX PROGRAM
PHASING OUT OF INVESTMENT TAX PROGRAM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the investment tax credit was instituted back in the mid-1970s. It turns out that the ITC was not intended to stimulate employment in the production of machinery and equipment. The purpose, according to Finance officials, was to enhance productivity by encouraging more investment in equipment.
Clearly, the ITC ought never to have applied to agriculture. The ITC is a program which encouraged wealthier farmers to flip equipment for tax purposes. It is a program which was not even intended to stimulate employment in the manufacturing of equipment in Canada, a program which did little to enhance productivity in western agriculture-a sector which is already highly productive. It is a program which has cost the Canadian Treasury hundreds of millions of dollars, moneys which might have been better used on other agriculture programs.
The investment tax credit was another Liberal program, like the scientific research tax credit-ill-conceived, poorly designed, and open to abuse.
I congratulate the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) for recognizing the ITC as a program without purpose and for acting to phase it out.

subsubtopic: OPPORTUNITY TO ESTABLISH NEW SPACE AGENCY IN MONTREAL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, for a number of weeks now Montreal has been urging that it be designated as the site of the space agency headquarters. Board of Trade President Manon Vennat and Chambre de commerce President Marcel Daoust have made strong representations to have the agency located in Montreal.
Yesterday's Le Devoir stated: "Space centre in Montreal considered as realistic and challenging vision for all Canada". This is a true statement, Mr. Speaker: 55 per cent of Canada's space industry is located in Montreal; 79 per cent of research and development is carried out in that region; 45 per cent of the space industry sales are made in Montreal. Montreal's four universities provide excellent synergy for academic and industrial circles.
Notwithstanding so many good reasons to make Montreal Canada's space agency centre, it would seem that this Government may be considering locating it elsewhere. I think it is a very important issue, and we have been told that there are several reasons for this, one being that some public servants in this sector would be reluctant to leave the national
capital, but I do not think this is a sufficient reason. The Government would be well advised to keep its mandate in mind and make sure that the country's economic interests come first, another way of suggesting that the space centre must be located in Montreal.

subsubtopic: REDUCTION IN NUMBER LIVING BELOW POVERTY LEVEL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, thanks to the effective policies of the Progressive Conservative Government, poverty in Canada is being significantly reduced. Statistics Canada reports that as real family income increases the number of Canadians living below the poverty line declined by 263,000 in 1985. For those of us of the Conservative persuasion who believe in the dignity of all mankind, this is welcome news.
[DOT] (UlO)
It is evident that the Government's emphasis on the creation of an economic environment which encourages investment, new jobs, and opportunity, is much more effective in eliminating hardship than the old Liberal-NDP approach of hand-outs and giveaways.

subsubtopic: BRITISH COLUMBIA BUDGET-CRITICISM OF PROVISIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, yesterday the British Columbia Government brought down a Budget that will cost average families an extra $135 in taxes. The Budget also provides strong evidence that the plan of the Conservative Government to ban new generic drugs will indeed hurt consumers.
The British Columbia Government has reached a new low in its treatment of the elderly by forcing seniors to pay 75 per cent of the dispensing fee for prescription drugs, up to $125 annually. Although there is compensation for the very poor, this will affect a great many seniors who live just near the poverty line.
The British Columbia Government has also hurt the elderly and sick by increasing the deductible for pharmacare. I submit that these callous actions are very much related to the drug Patent Act that will force families to pay more for prescription drugs. It is another example of Ottawa Conservatives working hand in hand with B.C. Socreds to make corporations wealthy at the expense of the elderly, the sick, and the poor.
March 20, 1987

subsubtopic: RESULTS OF SCIENTISTS' RESEARCH AND INNOVATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the easiest people to deride in this House are professors. No MP dares say a word against farmers, fishermen, industrial workers, or business people, provided that they are small. But anyone, any day, can run professors down without fear of retaliation.
Yet the cars people use to drive to work, the equipment with which they work, the economy that makes the work possible, and the satisfaction of almost every legitimate need result from the research and innovation of scientists and scholars, mostly at universities.
Here is a priority for all levels of government and all members of the private sector as we see the rising need for increased funding for research. Without it Canada could not have prospered in the 20th century, nor can it hope to advance in the 21st century.

subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF SPACE AGENCY AND SITUATION OF ELDERLY WORKERS WITH REGARD TO UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE
ESTABLISHMENT OF SPACE AGENCY AND SITUATION OF ELDERLY WORKERS WITH REGARD TO UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as my colleague from Outremont (Mrs. Pepin) just pointed out, the Chambre de commerce and Board of Trade of Montreal, the mayor of Montreal and, yesterday, Montreal editorial writers, the Quebec National Assembly-for the second time-the Opposition, the Parti quebecois and the Liberal Party unanimously endorsed a motion urging the Mulroney Government to confirm Montreal as our aerospace industry centre by establishing the space agency in Montreal.
Mr. Speaker, it is imperative, first, that at their Quebec City weekend meeting the Conservative Members general council adopt a unanimous resolution supporting Montreal; and, second, that the general council of Conservative Members should pass a unanimous motion aimed at eliminating unemployment insurance discrimination against elderly workers.

subsubtopic: SMALL CRAFT HARBOURS-CALL FOR INCREASED MAINTENANCE EXPENDITURES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Department of Fisheries has budgeted only $47.5 million for maintenance of small craft harbours. Mr. Mike Godin of the Harbour Maintenance Branch estimates that $120 million per year is needed. If we do not spend that amount of money, within five years we will have to close about 150 Class C fishing harbours.
In other words, the Government is not maintaining the basic infrastructure needed for both our fishing and tourist industries. In some cases if fire breaks out on fishing vessels it will be impossible for fire engines to have access. In the meantime licence fees for fishermen on the Pacific coast have doubled and, in some cases, wharfage rates have more than doubled.

March 20, 1987
Oral Questions
The Government must change this penny wise and dollar foolish policy of neglecting our basic fishing industry.

subsubtopic: BANK RATE REDUCTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is true that some regions of Canada are booming and others are not sharing equally in Canada's strong economic performance. However, there is one key development which helps every region, that is, lower interest rates.
Yesterday the Bank of Canada rate dropped to 7.14 per cent, the lowest in 14 years. When the Government came to power in September, 1984, the Bank of Canada rate was 12.38 per cent.
This is good news for all Canadians. It helps young couples acquire homes. Lower interest rates mean the creation of more small businesses and help existing ones to survive.
Lower interest rates even help the Government. Each 1 per cent decrease means an annual saving of over $2 billion in interest charges on the national debt. This helps reduce the deficit.
As Jackie Gleason used to say, "How sweet it is!"

subsubtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE NEGOTIATIONS-POSITION OF NDPLEADER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, you will recall that the Liberals proposed a very thoughtful amendment to the Government's free trade motion earlier this week. The amendment called for the protection of agricultural marketing boards, the Auto Pact, Canada's cultural industries, and other similar measures. The NDP voted against the amendment.
I have a transcript of an interview on CBC's The Journal of March 17 in which, in response to a question about free trade, the Leader of the NDP said:
Now if we're talking about a trading arrangement that has certain protective mechanisms, that keep in place marketing boards for our western farmers, that keep in place certain investment requirements in the automotive industry, that protect our cultural industries, in other words, all these exceptions, of course we could have a trade arrangement with the United States.
Mr. Speaker, the NDP will never be accused of telling the truth.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
subsubtopic: GOVERNMENT RESPONSIBILITY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, today, there are a number of articles in the Globe and Mail, Le Droit and Le Devoir about the Official Languages Act and the Government's intention to introduce a Bill. Today, Le Droit says that the Conservative Government-
-will provide bilingual services only in offices receiving an average of fifty requests per month, twelve months a year, in the minority language. In areas with a population of over 200,000, there will have to be more than 5,000 Francophones for Ottawa to provide services in both languages as a matter of course.
Mr. Speaker, Saskatoon, Saint John, New Brunswick and even Victoria do not have 5,000 Francophones, and I think their rights are going to be taken away. Why do the Conservatives feel they can afford to quantify the rights of Canadian men and women? This Government does not seem to realize that such a policy is prejudicial to the advancement of Francophones in several provinces.
We could say that this quantification policy is a sure sign of the Government's lack of any common sense. Mr. Speaker, when revising the Official Languages Act, the Government will have to set effective dates for language of service, language of work and language of communication, but it will also have to act responsibly to ensure that equitable representation is reflected in this Government and in this Parliament.
['Maybe the NDP would dictate to them. We will not.']

speakeroldname: Right Hon. John N. Turner (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I was going to offer my best wishes to the Prime Minister on his birthday, but he is not in the House.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. John N. Turner (Leader of the Opposition):
subsubtopic: UNITED STATES PRESIDENT'S PROMISES-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is therefor directed to the Deputy Prime Minister, because we are celebrating another anniversary as well. Exactly a year ago, the Prime Minister announced:
-We are now going to reduce air pollution. That will remain our immediate objective.
This week, however, the Prime Minister praised the President of the United States for the same promise he received from him last year and the year before, which was that he would look into the problem of acid rain. How many
March 20, 1987

times does he have to thank the President of the United States for promises the latter made and which he has yet to keep?

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister and President of the Privy Council):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Vice-President; President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subsubtopic: UNITED STATES PRESIDENT'S PROMISES-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I really find it strange that the right hon. gentleman opposite would want to be so critical of progress that is being made on a very, very important issue. He and his Party should be the last ones to condemn the actions of this federal Government in trying to make progress in resolving this very important national and international situation. The Liberal Government of the day walked away from the bargaining table of trying to work toward a permanent resolution.
Under the leadership of the Prime Minister and with the close co-operation of the U.S. administration progress indeed has been made, and it was so indicated in Mr. Reagan's statement when he said, "We've made some progress in learning things that can be done and we were ready to make this move. There are others probably yet to come. We're still investigating this." This is a positive reaction to a very important problem. The Right Hon. Leader of the Opposition and his Party should be commending our Government and the United States for this action rather than adopting that attitude.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. John N. Turner (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Deputy Prime Minister is contagiously close to the Prime Minister in attempting to rewrite history. The joint report of Drew Lewis and William Davis, the Special Envoys on Acid Rain reported that the amount of S02 emitted in 1983 represents a 28 per cent decline from the peak level emitted in 1973. Electric utility S02 emissions declined by 19 per cent between 1973 and 1983 and industrial emissions declined by 46 per cent. There was a lot of action under the previous Government which has not been continued under this administration.
My question relates to the fact that the Prime Minister has thanked the President for a giant step backward. In fact, even American Congressmen are criticizing our Prime Minister for undermining their efforts in the Congress to proceed toward emission control. Why has the Prime Minister backed away from his position of last year when he insisted on immediate emission controls?

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister and President of the Privy Council):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Vice-President; President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
Clearly, Mr. Speaker, progress has been made and if the right hon. gentleman would read the press release from Washington it makes clear reference to the fact that three major steps, consistent with the envoys' proposal, were being adopted and acted upon. Surely that is a clear indication not only of the commitment made south of the border but indeed of the progress being made
Oral Questions
which will be the subject of the bilateral talks to take place at the summit early in April. I know that the Right Hon. Leader has to play the role of being an opposition spokesman, but certainly when you are in opposition you have to have a little credibility.
Check with Dalton.

speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Vice-President; President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: The credibility that he and his Party have with respect to the actions they took on acid rain certainly does not give them much credibility and credence for the position they are taking right now.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext: It is a hell of a lot better than yours.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. John N. Turner (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I say this in a kindly way to the Deputy Prime Minister. He is not adding to his credibility by being a mouthpiece for his neighbour the Prime Minister of Canada.
Every school child knows that smokestacks and cars are a source of acid rain. Yet the President of the United States is thanked by our Prime Minister for conducting more research into the sources of acid rain. When will our Prime Minister tell the President of the United States, "We have the research. Let us get on immediately to emission controls"?

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister and President of the Privy Council):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Vice-President; President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, if the hon. gentleman is so sure we have all the research, why didn't he and his Government act prior to 1984? They did absolutely nothing. They walked away from the bargaining table. They refused to talk to the Americans. Within six months of taking office, with the co-operation of the provinces, we agreed to reduce emissions by 50 per cent. Through the efforts of the Prime Minister we have been successful in getting the U.S. discussions back on track. We have had very productive discussions and productive commitments. Those talks will continue at the summit.
The right hon. gentleman should acknowledge, as the Leader of the NDP did yesterday, that progress has been made. I am really surprised that the right hon. gentleman is so jealous of the progress that has been made.

Mr. Speaker, two hours ago in Quebec City the Quebec Government and the Government of Canada signed an acid rain agreement which is part of the process that was initiated by the Liberal Government in 1984, just to inform the Deputy Prime Minister.
Last night on television we heard President Reagan at his press conference saying the following:
We have found that the further we've gone, the more complex the issue of the
source of acid rain becomes.

March 20, 1987
Oral Questions
It does not seem to me that this is a statement by a person who is ready to act with acid rain clean-up programs. This is a stalling tactic. Does the Deputy Prime Minister not realize that the President has taken a stalling tactics approach?

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister and President of the Privy Council):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Vice-President; President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. gentleman, who is a former Minister of the Environment, should refrain from selective quotations to try to present a weak case. If he read further he would learn that the President said:
We've made some progress in learning things that can be done and we were
ready to make this move. There are others probably yet to come. We're still
investigating this.
I think that is a pretty positive statement.

Mr. Speaker, that is exactly our point. The progress that has been made in the mind of the President of the United States is that it is no longer volcanoes and ducks. That is the progress that has been made.

Mr. Speaker, it is a solid position common to all three Parties in this House that procrastination is not helping Canada. Therefore, will he make representations to the Prime Minister urging him to push for a North American acid rain agreement with deadlines, percentages and targets? Can he tell us when Canada will be protected by such a treaty?

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister and President of the Privy Council):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Vice-President; President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I do not have to make representations to the Right Hon. Prime Minister. He has clearly shown leadership and made progress in this regard. More leadership will be demonstrated at the summit and more progress will be made.

subsubtopic: FIRST MINISTER'S MEETING-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the Minister of Justice. Next Thursday there will be a major meeting of First Ministers and the aboriginal peoples of Canada to discuss aboriginal rights. The Minister knows that the federal Government has left leadership, with regard to documents that will be discussed, to the provinces which will determine the substance of the meeting.
At this late stage before the meeting starts next Thursday will the Government of Canada undertake to make public its position on the crucial issues to be discussed at that meeting?

speakeroldname: Hon. Ray Hnatyshyn (Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada):
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: FIRST MINISTER'S MEETING-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I appreciate very much the question asked by the Leader of the New Democratic Party
because it affords me the opportunity to restate once again the very great priority which the Prime Minister gives to this important meeting coming up next week.
I believe that impartial observers of this process will agree that throughout the consultation process and period the federal Government has consistently given leadership in terms of rolling drafts, in terms of stating the position of the federal Government up front, and in terms of trying to move the parties toward a constitutional amendment.
We are determined to arrive at an agreement if possible but it will require movement on the part of participants in these meetings. I call upon those who are participating to come to this meeting with an open mind in order that we may bridge the gaps which now exist between the parties in order to serve the true and legitimate interests of the aboriginal peoples of Canada.

subsubtopic: FIRST MINISTER'S MEETING-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, when you work your way through that fog you conclude that the federal Government is not prepared to state its position openly and therefore take a leadership role.

I would like to quote what the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development had to say on this and then ask the Minister to deal with the question. In the House on March 11 the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development said:
There has not been a proposal put forward in the meetings that has not been
supported by the federal Government when it came to trying to bring
consensus from all sides of the table.
The Minister is saying that the federal Government has not taken the lead. It is prepared to follow the lead of others and maybe get a consensus. Will the federal Government now show some leadership and, before next Thursday's meeting, publicly release its views, particularly on the crucial question of aboriginal self-government?

speakeroldname: Hon. Ray Hnatyshyn (Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada):
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the position put forward by the Leader of the NDP is patently absurd. The fact is that the federal Government has come a very considerable way and has tried to bring the participants along and make progress on the issue. We have taken a position with respect to the right of self-government which is clear and unequivocal. We are unequivocally supportive of the right of self-government. We want to, and on this all participants agree, determine the process by which self-government will be instituted in a constitutional way. We are the first Government to put forward our views with respect to financing and every other critical issue to be discussed at that meeting. There is no secret about our position. We are the leaders in putting our position forward.
March 20, 1987

Mr. Speaker, it is just unfortunate, and I will not go into the details now, that the leadership of virtually all the aboriginal peoples have been quite critical of the federal Government for failing to do precisely what the Minister claims it is doing.
I want to ask the Minister another question which came out of a House committee meeting last night. It has been suggested that the federal Government is now making changes in the proposed agenda for the first day. As the Minister knows, the first day was supposed to be allocated to discussions of the question of self-government. The suggestion now is that the federal Government is proposing a much more general discussion on the first day about a variety of aboriginal matters. Will the Minister clarify this situation? Is the Government still proposing to go ahead on the first day and deal with the very important matter of self-government?

speakeroldname: Hon. Ray Hnatyshyn (Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada):
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the agenda is under discussion now. The Prime Minister has written to the Premiers and leaders of the aboriginal groups represented at the conference. The federal Government cannot solve this matter unilaterally. A constitutional amendment is required. Not only the federal Government but seven provinces representing 50 per cent of the population must support it. It is not possible to have movement unless we have the support of the provincial Governments. I say to the Hon. Leader of the NDP that we have been giving leadership and striving mightily at the Ministers' meetings to bring about that kind of consensus on the best possible level so that the aboriginal peoples will be able to achieve self-government and realize their expectations in the Canadian confederation.

subsubtopic: RIGHTS OF EARLY RETIREES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Employment and Immigration. Next Monday, in Montreal, I am having a meeting with older workers to explain the decisions announced this week and what should be done to defend the rights of early retirees.
Could the Minister explain to the House why he decided to continue to discriminate against older workers who have company pension plans, as opposed to the older worker who has a registered retirement savings plan? Why is the older worker who has a company pension plan not entitled to full
Oral Questions
unemployment insurance benefits, while the worker who is getting money from a registered retirement savings plan is entitled to full unemployment insurance benefits? Why the double standard?

speakeroldname: Hon. Benoit Bouchard (Minister of Employment and Immigration):
subsubtopic: RIGHTS OF EARLY RETIREES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in November 1984, the Minister of Finance identified a set of rules dealing with the issue of simultaneous income from pensions and unemployment insurance. In these rules, the Minister of Finance considered that private pension plans were eligible and public pension plans were not.
At his meeting next Monday, I think the Hon. Member will have to make it clear that the Government has always maintained the same principle. There has never been any change in the Government's position in the way it deals with early retirees. However, for considerations of justice and equity in implementing the measure, the Government has decided to consider a refund for people who formally applied for unemployment insurance before 1986, but that will not be the case for those who applied after that time. I think this position is quite clear, and it will remain entirely in line with what was announced by the Minister of Finance in November 1984.

Mr. Speaker, I have a supplementary. The fact remains that the Minister has yet to explain why some older workers are treated better than others. The purpose of my supplementary is to get some information for these people. Could the Minister inform the House whether a person who on October 10, 1985 agreed with his employer to take early retirement and who because of separation payments and accumulated sick leave was not eligible for unemployment insurance benefits until February 10, 1986, is considered to be a 1985 retiree and thus eligible for the refund or will that person be penalized if he failed to apply at the time of termination of employment?

speakeroldname: Hon. Benoit Bouchard (Minister of Employment and Immigration):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think the statement I made in the House the day before yesterday was quite clear in this respect. I said that people who formally applied for unemployment insurance benefits at a Canada Employment and Immigration Centre before January 1986 would be considered. There are a number of special cases. The staff at the employment centres has a certain amount of leeway, and the usual mechanisms that exist at employment centres should people decide to protest the Government's procedures are in place and will apply in these instances. I want this to be quite clear. I repeat, people who formally applied for unemployment insurance benefits before January 5, 1986, will be considered.

March 20, 1987
Oral Questions

subsubtopic: ACID RAIN-UNITED STATES PRESIDENT'S PRESS CONFERENCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I would like to return to the Deputy Prime Minister and the issue of acid rain. The President of the United States, at his press conference, when asked about it, said "We are still investigating this". The President has some fine qualities, no doubt, but he is not known as a quick study. I ask the Deputy Prime Minister not to tell us about what the Liberals did in the past or anything else. I want to know whether the Canadian Government was satisfied with the President's response at that press conference yesterday?

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister and President of the Privy Council):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Vice-President; President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subsubtopic: ACID RAIN-UNITED STATES PRESIDENT'S PRESS CONFERENCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, we are certainly satisfied with the announced initiative and will, I am sure, be satisfied with the results of the continuing discussions which will take place between the Prime Minister and the President when they meet here in early April.

Mr. Speaker, 1 think most people in Canada think that acid rain is the key environmental issue in North America. They are really disappointed with our leaders on both sides of the border for their responses. Is the Deputy Prime Minister aware that a U.S. Congressman from Minnesota said this morning that our Prime Minister's dealings with the President on acid rain are retarding congressional efforts to deal with acid rain? Will the Government stop retarding the efforts of the anti-acid rain lobby by pretending that the President is doing something significant on acid rain when he is not? Would it not be better for the Government to work with congressional leaders against acid rain instead?

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister and President of the Privy Council):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Vice-President; President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I guess there is nothing wrong with different points of view being expressed in the U.S., just as they are expressed in Canada, on this very important issue. I remind the Hon. Member that there has been considerable progress not only on acid rain but on other fronts as well. For example, on February 4, 1987, Canada and the U.S., along with Ontario and New York, signed a declaration of intent which, coupled with the Niagara River management plan, will see a 50 per cent reduction of loadings of persistent toxic chemicals into the Niagara River by 1996. There was, in the fall of 1985, a joint declaration of intent regarding transborder control of hazardous wastes. There was a Memorandum of Understanding creating contingency measures for dealing with accidental and unauthorized discharges along the inland boundary.
That was not the President.

speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Vice-President; President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, last March 9 the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) rose in this House to observe Commonwealth Day. Barely a few days later we are proud to mark the anniversary of the creation of L'Agence de cooperation culturelle et technique (the Agency for Cultural and Technical Co-operation) on March 20, 1970 in Niamey, Niger, particularly in this year of the Quebec City francophone summit.
Canada, with Quebec alongside as a participating Government, was one of the founding members of the ACCT. New Brunswick joined the agency in 1977. Still today the ACCT is the most important Francophone intergovernmental organization.

Its initial vocation being the promotion of co-operation among member nations, through a common means of communications, the French language undoubtedly contributed to create the climate which led to the first meeting of heads of states and heads of governments held in Paris in 1986.
Indeed we can only be pleased that the growing number of Canadian representatives within the Agency for Cultural and
Technical Co-operation has paved the way, through such summits, for a formula which made it possible to invite the Premiers of Quebec and New Brunswick to attend these deliberations.
Before the Paris meeting, the Prime Minister (Mr. Mul-roney) stated in Montreal that:
-Canada's collective prosperity cannot be dissociated from the economic development of the Third World, industrial co-operation between countries and access to international markets.
He went on to say that:
-la Francophonie is a window on the world. It gives Canadian Francophones, whether they are from Quebec or any other province, the unlimited scope that those who speak English already have in the English-speaking world.

In 1987 Canada will host two major international meetings which will bring here representatives from more than 90 countries. Canada is one of the few countries which can claim to be a part of such a large international assemblage. In La Francophonie, as in the Commonwealth, most of Canada's partners are Third World countries. Our common interests require a greater measure of dialogue and co-operation in the face of the challenges before us.

The Quebec Summit, like the summit in Vancouver, will help enhance co-operation and understanding between countries and between heads of state of varying political affiliations and cultural origins, who nevertheless are able to converse in a common language. Canada, after ensuring that two of its provinces were allowed a degree of participation consistent with this country's constitutional framework, will spare no efforts to make this event a success that will ensure the further development of La Francophonie, an institution that reflects our most fondamental interests.

Mr. Speaker, I want to briefly raise a question of privilege of order with you regarding the long-standing practice of this House as explained to us in Beauchesne's Fifth Edition, Section 647, which reads as follows:
No act done at any committee should be divulged before it has been reported to the House.
This is a long-standing principle. It has also come to our attention through Erskine May's Twentieth Edition, on page 153, which reads as follows:
By the ancient custom of Parliament "no act done at any committee should be divulged before the same be reported to the House''.
Upon this principle the Commons, on 21 April 1837 resolved, "That the evidence taken by any select committee of this House, and the documents presented to such committee, and which have not been reported to the House, ought not to be published by any member of such committee or by any other person.''
On January 27, 1987, I apologized to this House for having accidentally released one line from a parliamentary committee report prior to it coming to the attention of the House of Commons. Those reports very accurately divulge the contents of the report. There is a further newspaper article on a similar issue involving the parliamentary committee dealing with day care. Yesterday there was a similar breach of parliamentary privilege, in my opinion, regarding another parliamentary committee dealing with unemployment insurance.
I want to close by asking that you investigate these matters and report to the House. I believe they could be breaches of our parliamentary privileges. All Members of this House have a right to be protected, otherwise we could all divulge the contents of these committee reports.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. John N. Turner (Leader of the Opposition) moved:
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-ABORIGINAL PEOPLES-CONSTITUTIONAL RIGHT TO SELF-GOVERNMENT
speechtext:
That this House affirms its support for the aboriginal peoples of Canada in their endeavour to have recognized in the Constitution their inherent right to self-government, and further instructs the Government of Canada to assume its leadership role and fulfil its Constitutional obligations to protect and guarantee the aboriginal and treaty rights of the aboriginal peoples of Canada, and specifically directs the Government of Canada to abandon its insistence that the right to self-government be contingent upon negotiated agreements.
He said: Mr. Speaker, the purpose of this motion is to urge the Government to correct what we believe is a historical injustice to the aboriginal people of our country. Before I proceed I want to pay tribute to the Hon. Member for
March 20, 1987

Cochrane-Superior (Mr. Penner) who will be following me in the debate from our side.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-ABORIGINAL PEOPLES-CONSTITUTIONAL RIGHT TO SELF-GOVERNMENT
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-ABORIGINAL PEOPLES-CONSTITUTIONAL RIGHT TO SELF-GOVERNMENT
speechtext:
He has been and continues to be a great friend of the aboriginal peoples of Canada. I think it is conceded that he is the leading authority in this House of Commons on the subject. It is thanks in large measure to his skill and persistence that this Party, both in Government and in opposition, has taken a leadership role on this issue.

And I am proud to lead the party that presided over the patriation of our Constitution and enshrined therein the rights of our aboriginal peoples. I want to pay tribute to the endeavour and perseverance of the aboriginal leaders who obtained constitutional recognition of their rights, and I salute their sustained efforts and determination to translate this recognition into a new framework for their relationship with Canada.
Finally, I had the privilege of meeting with Chief George Erasmus, and as I said to him at the time, we in the Liberal Party acknowledge that the right of our aboriginal peoples to self-government has existed for centuries. In fact, that right existed well before this continent was explored and colonized by the Europeans.
We believe that this right to self-government is inherent and has always existed, having never been extinguished. It exists today and should be recognized, therefore, in the Canadian Constitution.
At our convention last November this Party approved a resolution calling for the entrenchment in our Constitution of the right of our aboriginal people to self-government.

The Liberal Government led by my predecessor, Mr. Trudeau, also recognized that right. The Penner report, named after the Hon. Member for Cochrane-Superior, which recommended working towards the inclusion of aboriginal selfgovernment in the Constitution, was ordered by the Trudeau Government. Subsequent to this report, the same Government also introduced legislation to provide self-government for Indian nations.

As a result of that report, Mr. Trudeau also introduced a constitutional amendment to include aboriginal self-government in the Constitution. Mr. Trudeau's Government brought forward framework legislation for self-government for Indian nations. Aboriginal rights were included in the Constitution of 1982 along with the guarantee that those rights apply equally to men and women.
Supply
There was also recognition of the existence of rights acquired through both future and existing land claims agreements. Several land claims agreements were also negotiated including the self-government of the Cree-Naskapi in the James Bay area. Also included was the accord binding the federal and provincial Governments to hold three more conferences; one in 1984, one in 1985, and the conference next week, to reach agreement on this very critical issue for the aboriginal people of Canada.

We do not deny the complexity of this issue. We recognize the concerns it may raise for provincial Governments. However, we believe the federal Government should exercise its leadership to provide for aboriginal self-government, and in our opinion, the present Government is not exercising that leadership.

The issue turns on whether those rights should be included in the Constitution first as a general statement and affirmation of the rights of the aboriginal people which we consider to be inherent, never having been extinguished, or that all the details of every application of that right be worked out first and only then have the right included in the Constitution. It is the latter position which has been taken by the current Government of Canada. We believe it is the wrong one. The Government is attempting to make the right to self-government contingent upon the negotiation of successful agreements.
In his response dated March 18 to my letter of December 23, 1986, to the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) in which I requested that the Government pursue this matter, the Minister of Justice (Mr. Hnatyshyn) stated that the principle of self-government "would be enforceable in accordance with the terms of negotiated agreements in order to ensure the necessary certainty as to the potential scope and effect of aboriginal government jurisdiction".
In his telex to native leaders outlining the program for the upcoming conference the Prime Minister says they will not even discuss specifics. They will only chat about the concept of self-government and hope that possibly the lawyers can draft something they can all agree on-maybe. I quote from that telex as follows:
The first part of the conference will focus neither on the specific constitutional language nor on specific proposals.
That telex indicates that the Government is not only stepping backwards, but represents, I believe, an insult to the aboriginal people of the country. Let us remember where we were three years ago. I quote Mr. Trudeau at the First Ministers Conference in March, 1984, as follows:
The Government of Canada remains committed to the establishment of aboriginal self-government. . . .We are not here to consider whether there should be institutions of self-government, but how these institutions should be brought into being: what should be their jurisdiction, their powers; how they should fit into the interlocking system of jurisdiction by which Canada is governed.

March 20, 1987
Supply
In effect, the current Government is turning back the clock to before 1982. It wants to start all over again. How can our Government expect the aboriginal peoples to trust it? In our view this is simply not acceptable, not to the aboriginal people and not to the Party 1 represent today in the House of Commons, nor should it be acceptable to the other Members of the House of Commons.
We in the Liberal Party support a constitutional amendment which recognizes the inherent right, the historic right never extinguished, of the aboriginal people to self-government. The question for the Prime Minister and the Premiers next week is whether their vision of Canada is great enough to include the aboriginals' right to self-determination or whether they will once again insist on calling the shots.
Our First Ministers must demonstrate faith in the ability of the aboriginal peoples of this land to make their own decisions. It is not the time to take refuge in the security of what they may believe to be a status quo, that status quo having served the aboriginal people of this country so poorly in the past.
Not only must we have an acceptable amendment, we must also have a commitment from the Government subsequent to that amendment to negotiate and to provide the fiscal resources necessary for the effective exercise of self-government and a commitment to negotiate the necessary agreements and infrastructure. Our point is that the agenda should be, enshrinement of an existing right as a constitutional amendment to our constitutional position in 1982, then the infrastructure, then the agreements, then the financial underpinnings.
This is the last scheduled conference on the issue of aboriginal rights under the terms of the Constitution Act, 1982. Time is running out. I believe that we must move forward in the process started by my colleague, the Member for Cochrane-Superior, and continued by the last Government. The current Government cannot abrogate its responsibility to complete this historical and, I believe, essential change to our Constitution.
I am glad the Minister of Justice is here to respond. I understand his sincerity, but we believe that he ought to persuade his Government and the Premiers that this is the last constitutional opportunity under the law of 1982 to achieve that breakthrough. There are hundreds of thousands of Canadian citizens of aboriginal status awaiting his answer and looking forward to one last chance at that conference next week. We are counting on him, from our quarter of the House, to exercise on behalf of the people of Canada the leadership which I believe is overwhelmingly sought by Canadians everywhere and from every origin.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-ABORIGINAL PEOPLES-CONSTITUTIONAL RIGHT TO SELF-GOVERNMENT
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I am pleased to take part, on behalf of the Government of Canada, in this important debate.

Earlier today, the Leader of the New Democratic Party asked me to restate the position of the federal Government with respect to the very important issue we are debating today. It gives me a great deal of pleasure to participate in the debate so that I can state the federal Government's position on the matter of constitutional amendment on behalf of the aboriginal peoples of Canada.
Let me point out at the beginning that the position of the Government has been consistent since taking office. In fact, it
Supply
has been consistently better than that of Members opposite when they were in Government.
The Right Hon. Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Turner) is asking us to recognize an inherent right of self-government for aboriginal peoples. The previous Government refused to so in 1984. I am at a loss to understand why there should be such a blatant inconsistency on the part of the Official Opposition on this very important issue.
Indeed, I pointed out during the question and answer period with the Leader of the Opposition that, not only were the Liberals inconsistent between 1984 and today, they have been inconsistent between one and a half weeks ago and today.
It should be clear that the position of the Assembly of First Nations has been consistent throughout. From the very beginning they have insisted on the so-called inherent right to self-government. That certainly has not changed. The record will show, however, that that was a position they placed before the First Ministers' Conference of 1984, which everyone knew.
Let us look at what the Government of the day, many of whom are sitting in the Opposition now, said in response. In fact, I would like to quote from the federal proposal that was tabled at that conference. I refer to a particular provision from their proposed constitutional accord. It states:
The aboriginal peoples of Canada have the right to self-governing institutions that will meet the needs of their communities, subject to the nature, jurisdiction and powers of those institutions, and to the financing arrangements relating thereto, being identified and defined through negotiation with the Government of Canada and the provincial governments; and The Government of Canada and the provincial governments are committed to participating in the negotiations referred to in paragraph (B) and to presenting to Parliament and the provincial legislatures legislation to give effect to the agreements resulting from the negotiations.
That provision merely offered self-governing institutions and, moreover, it contained no guarantee that self-government arrangements would be constitutionally protected. The proposal then envisaged delegated powers that could have been revoked at any time by Parliament and the legislatures concerned.
So unsuitable was the Liberal Government's proposal that it prompted a caustic observation by a scholar and specialist on the subject of aboriginal constitutional rights. I want to quote from a recently published book by Dr. Bryan Schwartz of the University of Manitoba Law School, First Principles, Second Thoughts. He says:
The Federal Government's 1984 proposal on self-government was a brilliant public relations stroke. It was utterly vacuous; it contained no ideas on what self-government would look like in practice, no commitment to adequately fund them, no clarification of the federal-provincial division of powers and responsibilities in dealing with them. It was designed to be legally unenforceable. It might have prejudiced constitutional gains that aboriginal peoples had already made.
It would almost certainly have impeded their progress towards substantive constitutional assurances on self-government. Yet the impression created for the public was that the Federal Government had unveiled a bold new picture of aboriginal self-government.
What does that represent? Is that an inherent right? I do not think so. Is it a substantial acknowledgement of the right

March 20, 1987
Supply
in some way? I suggest that the answer is no. The proposal of the Liberal Government at the time was no more than a right to delegated legislation. It was not a constitutional solution. The negotiating climate established by the Government was so poor that even with this proposal it was only able to win the support of three provinces and, of course, none of the aboriginal associations. That record does not accord with the kind of proposition I hear from across the House today.
1 want to speak about our record in connection with this matter. When we took office we inherited an extremely polarized and very difficult situation. We moved immediately to reconcile two opposing points of view. On one hand, the aboriginal associations were insistent on an inherent right to self-government. On the other hand, many governments did not want to recognize any right of the aboriginal peoples to self-government in the Constitution. Instead, most governments preferred to proceed by non-constitutional means of defining self-government. They were led by the Liberal Government and the same Prime Minister whom the Leader of the Opposition now embraces, lock, stock and barrel. Mr. Trudeau's position was that he would give self-government but it would be delegated. It would be legislated rather than constitutionalized.
I know the Hon. Member for Cochrane-Superior (Mr. Penner) will agree that that proposition was patently absurd and unfair. While I thought he would have rejected it at the time, 1 did not hear him do so.
In December, 1984, my predecessor introduced a proposal that was designed to bring these two sides together in a spirit of compromise and negotiation which, I suggest, is the preferred way to work at constitutional development in our country. The polls indicate that this is what Canadians want. It is the preferred position of the aboriginal peoples. The proposal of my predecessor provided for the right of selfgovernment to be recognized in the Constitution subject to its detailed right being defined in agreements concluded by the governments and aboriginal representatives. That proposal marked the beginning of a new era in negotiating the right of the aboriginal peoples to self-government.
This has been a lengthy process involving numerous multilateral meetings at the ministerial level and at the level of officials. All parties worked together building upon this essential idea and identifying the components which they considered necessary to reach a workable agreement on a selfgovernment amendment.
As a result, the federal Government was in a position to table at the 1985 First Ministers' Conference a substantive and improved proposal for a constitutional amendment on aboriginal self-government. That proposal will have constitutionally committed Governments to negotiate self-government agreements with representatives of the aboriginal peoples. It also proposed and provided for the right to self-government set out in the agreements and that those rights would be given
constitutional protection. Despite its subsequent modification at the insistence of the Government of Saskatchewan, the proposal was supported in principle by seven provinces around the constitutional table and by two of the four aboriginal associations.
That represents the progress of the former Government and the present Government in constitutional amendment on behalf of the aboriginal peoples of Canada. I ask Hon. Members, particularly those who have put forward this proposition, to compare the two records and understand the progress which has been made.
The level of support from aboriginal associations for the proposals was not sufficient for Governments to proceed with an amendment without giving aboriginal peoples the opportunity to consult further with their constituents. However, the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) was not ready to give up. Instead, he asked aboriginal leaders to reconsider their positions and instructed his Ministers to convene a subsequent meeting to deal with the outstanding contentious items. The meeting took place, but the necessary support was unfortunately not forthcoming.
Since then the Government has been tireless in its efforts to pursue a constitutional amendment. It has convened and led numerous ministerial meetings to identify the necessary components of a workable agreement on the self-government amendment. It has also explored a number of options which might bring us to a compromise.
Throughout this very lengthy process we have attempted to strive for compromise, which is the essence of constitutional change. 1 have been a part of the process since July of last year and have participated in a series of not only multilateral meetings but a huge number of bilateral meetings with participants, with the purpose of seeing whether or not we could in fact establish appropriate wording for a constitutional amendment. The intervening period has been a productive one. We listened. We consulted. We negotiated and have been able to define, in my view, the essential shape of an agreement which will give us an amendment on self-government.
Let me be clear that the federal Government is prepared to support proposals which provide for the explicit recognition of the right of aboriginal peoples to self-government. We take the view that we must be equally explicit in ensuring that selfgovernment be implemented through agreements negotiated by Governments and the representatives of aboriginal peoples living in communities or regions, agreements tailored to the particular circumstances of aboriginal peoples which would encompass a broad range of matters.
We established a process of negotiation among aboriginal peoples and Governments to define and implement that right; to permit aboriginal control over matters that are directly affected and applicable to all aboriginal peoples; to ensure that the rights already recognized and affirmed in Section 35(1) of the Constitution Act, 1982 are neither diminished nor expanded; to permit the reasonable accommodation of the
March 20, 1987

interests and concerns of other Canadians; and, finally, to ensure that aboriginal peoples have access to the basic protections and privileges available to other Canadians.
1 want to review the approach of the Government. The Government supports an explicit statement, as I indicated before, of the rights of aboriginal peoples, and it would be implemented and exercised through a process of negotiations.
The recognition of the right would respect the aspirations of aboriginal peoples without compromising their position-and it is shared by most Governments-regarding the unacceptability of an immediately enforceable and inherent right to selfgovernment.
This position is based upon the strongly held view of Governments that the establishment of aboriginal selfgovernment should be achieved through negotiation. I suggest that the entrenchment of an inherent right could leave details of content and exercise to be decided by lawsuits and countersuits. Because these details of content and exercise refer to such complex items as the nature of the institutions of selfgovernment, their powers and jurisdiction, and financial arrangements, and because the arrangements resulting from negotiations could affect in many ways the lives of all Canadians, the Government and most others as well believe that they should be defined through negotiation.
Furthermore, the Government believes that a key purpose of self-government negotiations under an amendment is to develop new relationships between the two orders of government and the aboriginal peoples, thus establishing their rightful place in Confederation. The entrenchment of an inherent right and the inevitable litigation to define its content and exercise would not meet this goal.
The federal Government favours a process of negotiation to implement self-government. 1 think it is important to understand, however, that once agreements have been concluded, it believes that aboriginal self-government rights should be given constitutional protection. This is not a matter of passing legislation giving delegated self-government which can be revoked at the whim of any subsequent Parliament. This is constitutionalized self-government which has been arrived at by equal negotiation on the part of aboriginal peoples and the respective levels of Government. It would be constitutionalized and put out of the reach of subsequent Parliaments and the whims of subsequent legislators and subsequent governments, whether they be federal or provincial.
Constitutional protection of the rights contained in the agreements would safeguard them from unilateral amendment by Parliament or provincial legislatures. Having their rights thus recognized and affirmed is of special significance to Canada's aboriginal peoples.
Although it recognizes that in 1985 only six provinces were prepared to support it, the Government continues to believe that the commitment to negotiate self-government agreements should be placed in the constitutional amendment rather than in a political accord. This approach respects the aboriginal
Supply
belief that only a constitutionally mandated commitment to negotiate will guarantee the integrity of the process over a period of time and through changes of governments. While some governments have feared that a constitutionally mandated commitment would result in aboriginal groups resorting to the courts for rulings which would prescribe the terms of agreements where negotiations had failed, our view is that the commitment would simply require governments to negotiate in good faith.
We support the principle that the evolution toward and the financing of aboriginal self-government is a joint responsibility of both orders of government. Although we believe that the costs of self-government can only be determined on a case by case basis in the context of the powers and responsibilities which an aboriginal government would assume, we are of the view that neither level of government should off-load financial responsibilities as a result of self-government, and that both levels of government should share in any new costs resulting from the negotiations which would take place.
I have a couple of minutes left in which to deal with some very important issues. I hope the House will allow me a few minutes to conclude my remarks and entertain questions.
The position on the joint responsibility of both levels of government reflects a conviction shared by all governments that provincial participation is a practical necessity, given possible effects on areas of provincial jurisdiction. Provincial Governments have sought an active role in negotiation of selfgovernment agreements in order to ensure consistency by aboriginal self-governing communities with the standards and regulations in adjoining regions.

The Government supports the principle that Parliament and provincial Legislatures have a role to play in the constitutional protection of rights contained in their negotiated agreement.
[DOT] (M20)

A provision embodying this principle would require approval by the provincial legislature as well as Parliament in any case where rights set out in negotiated agreements were to obtain constitutional protection. This approval requirement reflects the positive role provinces are prepared to take in the negotiation and realization of self-government arrangements.
The Government is, however, willing to consider alternatives that do not involve provincial legislatures in the protection of rights contained in certain types of bilateral agreements. Certain of these alternatives have been advanced during the consultative process, primarily to the effect that provincial approval might not be required where their legislative jurisdiction or other interests were not affected.
We support the inclusion in an amendment of a nonderogation clause to ensure that new constitutional provisions could not be construed so as to derogate from any existing

aboriginal or treaty rights aboriginal peoples may have. Such a provision would guarantee that any new constitutional amendment would not prejudice the rights of aboriginal peoples that are now constitutionally recognized. At the same time, the amendment should ensure that existing rights are not expanded, except through a process of negotiated agreements.
The process that has led to this final conference has challenged the resourcefulness and perseverance of Governments and aboriginal associations alike. Although the search for constitutional change through negotiation has been a difficult one, the Prime Minister in his opening address to the 1985 First Ministers' Conference expressed confidence that:
The inventiveness and creativity that Canadians have always shown in
developing their democratic institutions-
-would stand participants in good stead.
The Government believes that significant tangible benefits would result from the federal approach to the constitutional recognition of aboriginal self-government rights. This approach would provide for self-government based on aboriginal peoples taking responsibility for their own decisions rather than having decisions made for them; based on self-reliance rather than dependence; based on pride and a sense of selfworth. This, indeed, is the Canadian way.

Madam Speaker, I thank the House for its indulgence. I will not be very long. I just wanted to put on record the full context of the background and the position of the federal Government for the benefit of Members and for the benefit of all Canadians.
If participants can achieve the level of agreement required for a constitutional amendment on aboriginal self-government, the federal Government believes that the door will have been opened to translating into reality the dreams of Canada's aboriginal peoples. In this sense, the Opposition's motion is not helpful as it is clearly not of a nature that could produce agreement to proceed with a constitutional amendment.

However, Madam Speaker, the Canadian Government's approach does not stop at that. Recently, we introduced a list of basic rules governing the financing of aboriginal governments.

Let me summarize what our approach does, Madam Speaker. First and foremost it asks that the aboriginal peoples of Canada give us none of their rights recognized within the Constitution. There are no risks in this regard for them. We
recognize those rights which are at present acknowledged by our Constitution.
Second, it provides for a solemn, indeed a constitutional commitment by governments to the aboriginal peoples that they will enter into negotiations aimed at concluding selfgovernment agreement.
Finally, it provides that the right to self-government identified in those agreements would be given constitutional protection. Let me stress what that means. It means protection in the highest law of this land.
Our approach would result in self-government arrangements based on negotiation and compromise. I think that is the route to follow in adjusting constitutional arrangements. I have to ask the question, and this, of course, is the nub of what we are talking about today: what does inherent right to self-government mean? Does it mean that we are going to dedicate the resolution of constitutional self-government to the courts and to a series of litigation by a variety of aboriginal peoples across Canada?
We have at the present time a very delicate and intricate jurisdictional relationship in Canada. It is appropriate and necessary for us to have a system which involves both levels of government in our country and the aboriginal peoples. Any amendment that would provide for an adjustment of those jurisdictional relationships must be formulated to ensure that that delicate balance is not thrown awry. The only way that I know of is through a process of doing it, what I call the Canadian way, through negotiation and agreement; a commitment to negotiate, a commitment with the aboriginal peoples enforceable in the courts of this land but nonetheless a political accord arrived at between the aboriginal people and the Governments of our country.
I agree with those who say that at the First Ministers' meeting we have a historic obligation no matter who we represent in those meetings to arrive at an agreement to set the basis for progress in the years ahead, to meet the legitimate hopes and aspirations of aboriginal peoples and to do it in a way which will ensure progress and ensure that the aboriginal peoples will realize self-government at the earliest possible moment in the most equitable way and in a way which will win the approval, not only of those peoples but of all peoples of Canada.
I thank you, Madam Speaker, for your time and for the indulgence of the House and I look forward to any questions that may be asked.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-ABORIGINAL PEOPLES-CONSTITUTIONAL RIGHT TO SELF-GOVERNMENT
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, all Members recognize the need for provincial consent. What troubles Members on this side and the aboriginal leaders is the lack of leadership shown by the federal Government. I want to ask the Minister why the Prime Minister of Canada (Mr. Mulroney) would suggest that the first day of the meeting be given over to a discussion of issues in a general way and that they not get down to specifics? It leaves the impression there are no specifics to be discussed. I believe what the Right Hon. Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Turner) is proposing in his motion today is similar to the Nova Scotia proposal which has a free-standing right in Section 35(5)(a). It stands on its own. It then goes on in Section 35(5)(b) to say the scope of the right shall be set out in agreements. That is quite different from the federal position which at the very outset wants to make the right contingent.
My second question is to ask why the Minister wants to raise this smoke-screen, along with other attorneys-general across the country, that a recognition of the right to self-government is going to mean a headlong rush to the courts. Surely the Minister is now well enough acquainted with aboriginal leaders to know that it is not in the courts that they wish to seek a remedy but through negotiated agreements. If they wanted to use the courts, Section 35 gives them all the scope they need. There has been precious little of that except in the

Province of British Columbia which has been so reluctant to do any kind of negotiating at all.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-ABORIGINAL PEOPLES-CONSTITUTIONAL RIGHT TO SELF-GOVERNMENT
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I thank the Hon. Member for his questions. I should preface my remarks by acknowledging his very sincere interest in this matter over a long period of time. I do listen with interest and sincerity to his representations.
His first question dealt with the agenda. Reference has been made to a general discussion. I think that is taken out of the context of the Prime Minister's telex to the provincial Premiers and leaders of the aboriginal groups. There is specific reference to the draft proposed by Nova Scotia which is draft number three with an appendix. This document in itself has been the subject of discussions and it touches on all the salient and essential ingredients which have to be considered in coming to an agreement.
What we must do at the meeting and what the Prime Minister is interested in doing is having a discussion to resolve in a conceptual way some of those areas in which we can come together and bridge the gaps which have existed up until this point in time. I think the format will be helpful in arriving at a specific and detailed discussion so that an agreement can come out of the process.
The second question dealt with what is meant by inherent right. The Hon. Member puts forward the proposition that somehow the reason we are discussing the question of a process involving negotiations is that we are concerned that under the status quo, or indeed under an inherent right proposition, there will be a headlong rush, I think were his words, to the courts. With all due respect, 1 think this is a misunderstanding of the position we have put forward.
If you want to be quite candid and frank about the federal Government's position, this enhances the right of aboriginal peoples to go to the courts. It gives them an additional dimension, what I call a constructive and positive dimension, inasmuch as in the amendments put forward by the federal Government we include a commitment by the Government to negotiate. If we are simply silent or talk about inherent right or have some general reference to inherent right, that will fall far short of providing guidelines or any assistance to the courts to define what self-government really is. I ask the Hon. Member, and I referred to this the other day during Question Period, does he think that the courts are the appropriate forum

Supply

That is the mature political way in which we accomplish things in Canada. What I am saying to the Hon. Member is simply this. What I am looking for is to convince people that we should have the determination and will to look for creative wording.
